meta.titre: Astrogeology: the solar nebula, small bodies and the planets
meta.sous_theme: Origin and members of the Solar System

sections.contenu_markdown: On a clear night in Cameroon a bright streak crosses the sky for a second. People call it a falling star, but it is a particle of rock or metal burning up high in the atmosphere. Astrogeology applies the methods of geology to the Moon, the planets, asteroids and meteorites, and it asks the same questions as the rest of the subject: what is this made of, how did it form and how old is it? At GCE Advanced Level the marks are won on exact vocabulary (nebula, asteroid, meteor, comet) and on a clear account of the origin of the Solar System.

items: The Sun is a star and the Earth is one of the planets that orbit it.
Gravity pulls masses together, and during melting the denser materials sink while the lighter ones rise.
Density is mass divided by volume, and iron and nickel are far denser than common silicate rocks.
Hydrogen and helium are the commonest elements in the universe.

sections.titre: Origin and members of the Solar System
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Origin: the nebular hypothesis
The Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a **nebula**, a cloud of gas (mainly hydrogen and helium) and dust. The cloud contracted under its own gravity, spun faster as it shrank and flattened into a rotating disc with a hot, dense centre that became the Sun. Dust grains in the disc stuck together into **planetesimals**, which collided and grew by **accretion** into planets. The evidence: the planets orbit in the same direction and nearly in one plane, and the Sun spins in that direction; meteorites and the oldest Moon rocks give ages of about 4.5 to 4.6 billion years; discs of gas and dust are seen around young stars. The Big Bang explains the origin of the universe (about 13.8 billion years ago), not of the Solar System.

In the hot inner disc only rock and metal could condense, giving small, dense **terrestrial planets**. Farther out, ices also condensed, cores grew large enough to attract hydrogen and helium, and the **giant planets** formed.

### Members of the Solar System
| Body | Definition and key features |
|---|---|
| Terrestrial planets | Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars: small, rocky and dense, with a metallic core |
| Giant planets | Jupiter and Saturn (gas giants), Uranus and Neptune (ice giants): large, low density, deep atmospheres, rings |
| Dwarf planets | Orbit the Sun and are rounded but have not cleared their orbit, for example Pluto and Ceres |
| Asteroids | Rocky or metallic bodies that orbit the Sun, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter; left-over planetesimals |
| Comets | Bodies of ice, dust and rock from the cold outer Solar System; near the Sun the ice vaporises to give a coma and a tail that points away from the Sun |
| Meteoroid, meteor, meteorite | Meteoroid: a small particle in space. Meteor: the streak of light as it burns in the atmosphere. Meteorite: a piece that reaches the ground |

### Meteorites and the Moon
Meteorites are **iron** (iron-nickel alloy), **stony** (silicates) or **stony-iron**. Stony meteorites called chondrites contain small round grains (chondrules) and are primitive material, used to date the Solar System. Iron meteorites are thought to come from the cores of bodies that melted and differentiated, with dense metal sinking to the centre. The leading hypothesis for the Moon is the giant impact: a Mars-sized body struck the early Earth and the debris formed the Moon. The Moon's surface is heavily cratered because it has no atmosphere or running water to erase impact craters.

variantes.quand_utiliser: A question says 'define' or 'distinguish' for astrogeological terms.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Build each definition in three parts: the category (rocky body, icy body, particle, cloud), its key feature (composition, size, behaviour) and its location or origin (belt, outer Solar System, atmosphere). One sentence per term is enough. When terms are close, such as meteor and meteorite, state clearly what separates them: one is a light effect in the air, the other is a solid object on the ground.

variantes.quand_utiliser: A question asks for similarities and differences between the two groups.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Feature | Terrestrial planets | Giant planets |
|---|---|---|
| Position | Inner Solar System | Outer Solar System |
| Size and density | Small, high density | Large, low density |
| Composition | Rock and iron | Mostly hydrogen and helium, or ices |
| Surface | Solid | No true solid surface; very deep atmosphere |
| Moons | Few or none | Many |

Explain the difference by temperature in the early disc, not by a list alone.

variantes.quand_utiliser: A question asks which hypothesis explains an origin and why.
variantes.contenu_markdown: State the hypothesis, give its main steps in order, then support it with two or three pieces of evidence (same direction of orbits, ages of meteorites, discs around young stars). Mention a rival idea, such as a close encounter between two stars, only briefly and only as an idea that is no longer accepted.

sections.enonce_markdown: Explain why the planets of the Solar System orbit the Sun in the same direction, and why the planets nearest the Sun are small and rocky while those far from it are large and rich in gas. (8 marks)

etapes.action: Read the command word and split the question.
etapes.justification: 'Explain' means give causes, not just describe. There are two parts: the common direction of orbit and the difference between inner and outer planets.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Part 1: direction (about 3 marks). Part 2: inner and outer planets (about 5 marks).

etapes.action: Answer part 1 with the nebular hypothesis.
etapes.justification: The direction of the planets' motion must be traced to the material they formed from.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The nebula was rotating; as it contracted under gravity it spun faster (the same direction was kept) and flattened into a disc; the Sun formed at the centre; planets formed from the disc, so they orbit in the same direction and nearly in the same plane.

etapes.action: Explain the temperature difference in the disc.
etapes.justification: Planetary composition depends on what could condense where.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Near the Sun the disc was hot, so only rock and metal condensed; far from the Sun it was cold enough for ices to condense as well.

etapes.action: Explain the consequences for size and composition.
etapes.justification: Planet size depends on how much solid material was available to build a core.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Inner planets grew from scarce rock and metal, so they are small, dense and rocky. Outer cores gained ice as well as rock, grew massive enough to capture hydrogen and helium, and became large gas-rich giants.

etapes.action: Finish with one supporting piece of evidence.
etapes.justification: A short piece of evidence turns an assertion into an argument.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Meteorites give ages of about 4.6 billion years, matching a single time of formation.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The planets formed from a rotating disc of gas and dust that flattened out of a contracting nebula, so they orbit in the same direction in nearly the same plane. In the hot inner disc only rock and metal could condense, producing small, dense, rocky terrestrial planets. In the cold outer disc ices condensed as well, so cores grew larger, captured hydrogen and helium and became gas-rich giants. Meteorite ages of about 4.6 billion years support the idea of a single time of formation.

items.erreur_markdown: The Solar System was formed in the Big Bang.
items.pourquoi_faux: The Big Bang is the origin of the universe about 13.8 billion years ago. The Solar System formed much later, about 4.6 billion years ago, from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust.
items.correction_markdown: State that the Solar System formed from a nebula, and keep the Big Bang for the origin of the universe.

items.erreur_markdown: A meteor, a meteoroid and a meteorite are the same object.
items.pourquoi_faux: They name three stages: the particle in space, the streak of light in the atmosphere, and the fragment on the ground.
items.correction_markdown: Meteoroid in space; meteor as a flash of light in the atmosphere; meteorite on the ground.

items.erreur_markdown: A comet's tail trails behind it like the smoke of a moving train.
items.pourquoi_faux: The tail is produced by solar radiation and the solar wind, so it points away from the Sun, even when the comet moves toward the Sun.
items.correction_markdown: Say that the tail always points away from the Sun and is made of gas and dust released from the vaporising ice.

items.erreur_markdown: Asteroids are found in a belt between the Earth and Mars.
items.pourquoi_faux: The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
items.correction_markdown: Give the position as between Mars and Jupiter.

items.pourquoi_faux: Pluto has not cleared its orbit of other bodies, so since 2006 it has been classed as a dwarf planet.
items.correction_markdown: Name eight planets and describe Pluto as a dwarf planet.

items.enonce_markdown: Give the correct term for each of the following. (a) The streak of light produced when a sand-grain-sized particle burns up in the atmosphere. (b) A piece of space rock that survives and lands on the ground. (c) A rocky body, up to hundreds of kilometres across, that orbits the Sun between Mars and Jupiter. (d) A small icy body that develops a tail when it approaches the Sun.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Meteor.** (b) **Meteorite.** (c) **Asteroid.** (d) **Comet.**

Award a mark for each correct term.

items.enonce_markdown: Take the Sun-Earth distance as $1.5\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{km}$ and the speed of light as $3.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. (a) Calculate the time in seconds and in minutes for sunlight to reach the Earth. (b) Jupiter is $5.2$ times as far from the Sun as the Earth. Calculate the light travel time from the Sun to Jupiter in minutes.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $t=\dfrac{d}{c}=\dfrac{1.5\times10^{8}}{3.0\times10^{5}} = 500\ \mathrm{s}$, and $\dfrac{500}{60}=8.3\ \mathrm{min}$: **$500\ \mathrm{s}$, about $8.3\ \mathrm{min}$**.

(b) The distance is $5.2\times1.5\times10^{8} = 7.8\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{km}$, so $t=\dfrac{7.8\times10^{8}}{3.0\times10^{5}} = 2600\ \mathrm{s}$, and $\dfrac{2600}{60}=43.3\ \mathrm{min}$: **about $43\ \mathrm{min}$**.

items.enonce_markdown: A meteorite found in a field has a mass of $234\ \mathrm{g}$ and a volume of $30\ \mathrm{cm^{3}}$. Typical densities are about $3.3\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ for a stony meteorite and about $7.8\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ for an iron meteorite. (a) Calculate the density and classify the meteorite. (b) Name its probable composition. (c) Explain the probable origin of this kind of meteorite. (d) Suggest why this kind is over-represented among meteorites found rather than seen to fall.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Density $=\dfrac{234}{30}=7.8\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$, matching an **iron meteorite**.

(b) An iron-nickel alloy.

(c) It probably came from the metallic core of a parent body that was large enough to melt and differentiate, with dense metal sinking to the centre; later collisions broke up the body.

(d) Iron meteorites survive weathering far better than stony ones, which crumble, and they look unlike local rock, so they are noticed and recognised.

items_markdown: The nebular hypothesis: a rotating cloud of gas and dust contracted, flattened into a disc, formed the Sun and then planets by accretion of planetesimals, about 4.6 billion years ago.
Inner planets are small and rocky because only rock and metal condensed near the Sun; outer planets grew large cores and captured hydrogen and helium.
Meteoroid (in space), meteor (the light streak) and meteorite (on the ground) are different things; asteroids lie mainly between Mars and Jupiter.
A comet is an icy body whose tail of gas and dust points away from the Sun; Pluto is a dwarf planet.
Meteorites are iron, stony or stony-iron; chondrites are primitive and date the Solar System; the Big Bang belongs to the universe, not the Solar System.
